title: Alcohol and other substances: pattern, control, withdrawal and safety
about: Substance-use questions (42 CFR Part 2): answers stay in this session's memory only and are never sent or stored. They cover the drinking pattern, control over cannabis, opioids and stimulants, withdrawal and overdose safety (medical safety issues), and whether mood, anxiety or sleep problems predate or outlast heavy use.

questions.text: Ask about drinking: how often, how much on a typical day, and how often there are heavy-drinking days.
questions.why: A quick pattern check shows whether alcohol could explain or worsen sleep, mood or anxiety, and whether a fuller assessment is needed. Ask without judgment; many people underestimate their intake.

options.label: Drinks more than intended, or has frequent heavy-drinking days

questions.text: When the client cuts down or stops drinking, do they get shaky, sweaty, sick, very anxious or confused, or have they ever had a seizure or seen things that were not there?
questions.why: Alcohol withdrawal can be medically dangerous (seizures, delirium). If these signs are present, arrange an urgent medical assessment before any change in drinking, and do not advise stopping suddenly without medical support.

questions.text: Did the mood, anxiety or sleep problems start before the heavy drinking, or do they continue through long alcohol-free stretches (about a month or more)?
questions.why: Symptoms that start only with heavy drinking or withdrawal often ease within weeks of stopping; symptoms that came first or persist without alcohol suggest an independent problem that needs its own care.

options.label: Started before, or continue when not drinking
Only during heavy drinking or soon after stopping

questions.text: Ask how cannabis use has gone lately: control, cravings or withdrawal, and problems it causes.
questions.why: Regular cannabis use matters for anxiety, mood, sleep and motivation. Control, cravings or withdrawal, and use that continues despite harm show whether use has become a problem in its own right. Ask without judgment.

options.label: Uses more or for longer than planned, or cannot cut down
Craves it, or gets irritable, sleeps poorly or loses appetite when stopping
Keeps using despite problems at work, study, home or with mood

questions.text: Ask how opioid use has gone lately: control, cravings or withdrawal, and problems it causes.
questions.why: Loss of control and withdrawal show whether opioid use has become a problem in its own right, and they open the conversation about medication treatment, which saves lives. Ask without judgment, including about prescribed opioids.

options.label: Uses more than planned or prescribed, or cannot cut down
Aches, sweating, yawning, runny nose or stomach upset and strong cravings when stopping
options.note: Opioid withdrawal is rarely dangerous on its own but drives return to use; discuss medication for opioid use disorder.

questions.text: Ask how stimulant use has gone lately: control, cravings or withdrawal, and problems it causes.
questions.why: Stimulant crashes can look like depression, and heavy use can bring paranoia or panic. Control, the crash and use despite harm show whether use has become a problem in its own right.

options.label: Binges, uses more than planned, or cannot cut down
Craves it, or crashes when stopping (exhaustion, long sleep, low mood)
Keeps using despite heart, mental health, work or relationship problems

questions.text: Ask about overdose safety: a past overdose, using alone, a supply that may contain fentanyl, mixing with alcohol or sedatives, or a recent break from use.
questions.why: These raise the chance of a fatal overdose, and a recent break (jail, detox, treatment) lowers tolerance. The app records only what you choose and never estimates risk; talking through naloxone and not using alone is the step that matters.

options.label: A past overdose
options.note: Talk through naloxone, not using alone and what to do in an emergency; the overdose safety handout can help.

options.label: Uses alone, mixes with alcohol or sedatives, or the supply may contain fentanyl
options.note: Talk through naloxone, not using alone and what to do in an emergency; the overdose safety handout can help.

options.label: A recent break from use (jail, detox or treatment)
options.note: Tolerance drops quickly after a break: the usual amount can now be fatal.
